title: Sketching for ideas: loose ideation, ugly first drafts and iteration speed
summary: This module trains the habit of making many fast, rough drawings to find ideas instead of trying to produce one good drawing. You learn to treat early sketches as disposable thinking, set small constraints so you never face a blank page, and push past the first obvious idea by varying one thing at a time.
learning_outcomes: Fill a page with 20 or more quick variations of one subject without erasing or judging them
Set your own constraints (time, shape, subject, tool) so you can start drawing within a minute
Explain why the first idea is rarely the best and how to push past it by changing one variable
Choose which rough to develop using a stated reason rather than a hunch
Draw something from memory, notice where memory fails, and know when you need reference

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint Free Video Library: Study Habits and Theory & Mindset sections (What Should I Draw Today?, Generating Ideas, Give Yourself Assignments, Loosen Up, Letting Go, Start Anywhere)
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free, and a new one was said to appear every Tuesday and Thursday. A separate Premium Series ($10 videos, for example Playbook 16 Machine Design) is sold in the store and is not in this list. Individual lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Watch in this order: What Should I Draw Today? (Feb 2012, how choosing a subject can be harder than drawing it), Generating Ideas (Sept 2012, invent narrow fake assignments; the page links the donjon and Chaotic Shiny random generators), Give Yourself Assignments (Jan 2013, act as your own art director and impose a few limits). Then dip into Loosen Up (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/loosen-up), Letting Go (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/mastering-the-art-of-letting-go), the blog post Start Anywhere (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/blog/start-anywhere) and, from the Drawing 2 section, When in Doubt Draw 100 (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/draw-100) and Real Object, Imaginary Details (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/real-object-imaginary-details). I opened the first three pages; the others are listed on the library page but I did not open them.

resources.title: Training Yourself to Draw From Imagination, Part 1
resources.credit: Peter Han (entertainment designer, illustrator, author of Dynamic Bible)
resources.free_notes: The lesson page shows no price, paywall or parent course. It was recorded at the Proko booth at Lightbox Expo. Not explicitly labelled free, so treat as free but unconfirmed.
resources.notes: Watch Han build an invented fantasy character (a dwarf and a hog) while talking through his decisions, then finish with line work and ink shadows. The notes page does not list his steps, so the value is in watching how he explores shapes before committing. Duration not shown on the page.

resources.title: Gurney Journey: Preliminary Sketches label
resources.free_notes: Blog is free and a January 2026 post says it runs with no paywalls; a Substack edition exists. The Permissions section allows non-commercial quoting with credit and a link. His books and video courses are separate paid products and are not linked here.
resources.notes: Use the sidebar label list (Preliminary Sketches had about 75 posts when checked). Read a handful of posts that show a rough sketch next to the finished piece, and note how many rough ideas came first. I opened the home page only; the label page itself is blocked to automated fetching.

resources.title: Muddy Colors
resources.credit: Collective of 20+ fantasy and illustration artists
resources.free_notes: The site describes itself as a free online resource with a new article daily; it asks readers to support it on Patreon. Individual artists may sell their own courses elsewhere.
resources.notes: Browse for process articles in which working illustrators show early thumbnails and rough explorations. The home page showed posts on starting with small thumbnail sketches and on the creative process; I did not verify individual article quality.

practice.title: Twenty ugly sketches in twenty minutes
practice.description: Pick one ordinary subject (a kettle, a hat, a house). Make 20 one-minute sketches, a new angle or silhouette each time, with no erasing and no looking back. Circle the three most interesting afterwards.

practice.title: Draw 100 variations of a simple thing
practice.description: Choose a simple object and draw 100 small versions of it over several sittings, changing proportion, silhouette or detail each time. The point is to run out of easy ideas and keep going. See the When in Doubt Draw 100 video on Ctrl+Paint for the original idea.
practice.dose: 100 small drawings across 5 sessions of 15 min

practice.title: Self-assigned brief with three limits
practice.description: Act as your own art director: write a one-line subject, then add three limits (for example 10 minutes, only triangles, only a ballpoint pen). Complete it without breaking a limit. Repeat with a new brief. The Give Yourself Assignments video describes the approach.

practice.title: Memory first, reference second
practice.description: Draw a bicycle, a hand or a street lamp from memory in 5 minutes. Then look up a photo and mark in a second colour every place memory got the structure wrong. This shows exactly what you need to collect reference for.

practice.title: Same sketch at 5, 2 and 1 minute
practice.description: Draw one idea three times against a timer at 5, 2 and 1 minute. Compare what survived as the time shrank; that is the part of the idea that matters most.

done_when: You can fill a page with 20 distinct rough variations of one subject in about 20 minutes without erasing
When you sit down with no idea, you write a three-limit brief and start drawing inside one minute
You can say why you picked one rough over the others in a single sentence that is not 'it looks nicest'
You have at least 100 rough drawings in a sketchbook and have not thrown any away
common_mistakes: Polishing the first sketch because it feels promising, which ends the exploring early
Erasing during the ideation phase, which slows you down and makes each mark feel precious
Varying everything at once, so you cannot tell which change helped; change one variable per round
Waiting for inspiration instead of imposing constraints and starting

school_reference.institution: FZD School of Design (Singapore)
school_reference.note: Its one-year programme opens with a fundamentals term (the site also lists free articles such as Sketching 101) before moving on to idea generation from reference.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA
school_reference.note: Its Visual Development emphasis is described as high volume with quick turnarounds, which is the working pace this module rehearses.

title: Composition fundamentals: focal point, balance, rhythm, thirds, leading lines, framing and negative space
summary: Composition is how you arrange shapes, values and edges so the viewer's eye lands where you intend and moves through the picture on purpose. You study the standard devices (focal point, balance, repetition and rhythm, thirds, leading lines, framing, negative space) and learn to spot tangents and clutter that work against them.
learning_outcomes: Find the focal point of an unfamiliar image and name the contrasts that create it
Use symmetrical and asymmetrical balance, repetition and rhythm, and movement deliberately
Apply thirds, leading lines, framing elements and negative space as tools rather than formulas
Spot and remove tangents and accidental overlaps
Critique a composition in plain language

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint Composition Basics: Principles of Design series, Visual Simplification, Visual Tangents, Framing Elements, Shadow Shape
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free. A separate Premium Series ($10 videos) is sold in the store and is not part of this list. Individual lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Watch in the order the library lists them: Principles of Design Intro (Dec 2011), Scale and Proportion, Repetition (rhythm), Emphasis, Balance, Movement, Unity (slugs follow https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/principles-of-design-balance and similar), then Visual Simplification (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/visual-simplification), Visual Tangents (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/avoiding-visual-tangents), Compositional Framing Elements (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/compositional-framing-elements, Mar 2012), Shadow Shape (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/shadow-shapes) and the Critique video. The Photoshop references are incidental; the design principles are tool-independent. I opened the intro and framing lessons; the rest are taken from the library listing.

resources.title: Gurney Journey: Composition label (about 105 posts)
resources.free_notes: Blog is free and a January 2026 post says it runs with no paywalls. The Permissions section allows non-commercial quoting with credit and a link. His books and video courses are separate paid products and are not linked.
resources.notes: Use the Composition label in the sidebar and read short worked examples in date order, about 10 posts. The label page is blocked to automated fetching, so I confirmed the label and its post count from the home page only.

resources.title: Tate Art Terms: Composition
resources.free_notes: Free to read on tate.org.uk. Tate site terms apply to reuse of text and images.
resources.notes: A short definition (the arrangement of elements within a work) with the historical contrast between classical triangular or pyramidal layouts and later 'allover' composition. Read it for vocabulary and to see that the thirds-and-triangles toolkit is one tradition among several.

resources.title: Creative Composition (Will Terry), School of Visual Storytelling
resources.free_notes: Only available through an SVSLearn subscription ($180 per 6 months billed monthly, or $300 per year). There is a 14-day free trial that needs a credit card and renews automatically unless cancelled. No standalone course price or free preview was shown.
resources.notes: 51 lessons, about 4 hours of video. Page lists: four principles of design, planning an image with them, legibility, simplifying complex images, a hierarchy of focal points, and thumbnails through to a finished drawing. Included because Will Terry is a well-known composition teacher; use the trial only if you will cancel in time.

practice.title: Dissect ten images into flat shapes
practice.description: Choose ten paintings from an open-access museum collection or ten film stills. For each, draw a small rectangle and block in 3 to 5 flat shapes showing where the big masses sit, then mark the focal point with a dot and note in a few words what attracts the eye (contrast, edge sharpness, size, position).

practice.title: One set of shapes, five layouts
practice.description: Gather five to seven simple shapes. Arrange them in five small frames, each aiming at a different device: symmetrical balance, asymmetrical balance, rhythm through repetition, a thirds placement, and a frame within a frame. Write one line under each saying what you changed.

practice.title: Tangent hunt on your own sketches
practice.description: Take three of your older sketches or photos and mark every place where two edges just touch or line up awkwardly. Redraw each quickly with the problem edges overlapped or separated.

practice.title: Same scene, three ways to make the focus
practice.description: Draw one simple scene (a figure in a doorway) three times in tiny frames. In the first make the focal point with value contrast, in the second with edge sharpness, in the third with size and position. Compare which reads fastest from across the room.

practice.title: Negative space silhouette scene
practice.description: Design a small scene where the empty area is the main shape: a lone tree on a hill, a doorway, a tiny person under a huge sky. Do four versions varying how much empty space surrounds the subject.

done_when: You can name the focal point of an unseen image within a few seconds and give two reasons for it
Your last five thumbnails have no unintended tangents
You can produce, on request, a version of one scene that is balanced symmetrically and another that is balanced asymmetrically
You can explain in one sentence when you would deliberately break the thirds guideline
Someone else can point to your intended focal point without being told
common_mistakes: Putting the main subject dead centre by default and splitting the frame into equal halves
Treating the rule of thirds as a law and placing subjects on intersections mechanically
Giving every area equal contrast and detail, so there is no hierarchy
Ignoring the frame edge and filling every gap, so shapes get cut awkwardly and calm areas never support the focus

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA
school_reference.note: Its curriculum is described as starting with visual storytelling, colour theory, composition and anatomy before students choose an emphasis in third year.

school_reference.institution: CalArts, Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: First year pairs life drawing with colour and design and storytelling classes; students make one short film per year, which is where composition gets used in motion.

title: Thumbnailing and compositional sketching
summary: Thumbnails are tiny, fast drawings used to try many compositions before committing to a large one. You practise reducing a scene to a few value shapes, generating lots of variations quickly (including by cutting up and rearranging them), and picking the strongest on purpose.
learning_outcomes: Produce a dozen distinct thumbnails of one brief in under 30 minutes
Reduce a scene to two or three values so the layout reads at small size
Vary camera angle, crop and shape arrangement, not just where objects sit
Combine or remix thumbnails to create new ideas
Select one thumbnail to develop and say why

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint thumbnail videos: Modular Thumbnail Sketches, Thumbnail Iteration, Chop and Warp, Imaginary Landscape Thumbnails, The Tiny Study
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. Individual lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: In order: The Tiny Study (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/the-tiny-study, reduce a photo to colour patches), Imaginary Landscape Thumbnails (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/imaginary-landscape-thumbnails, small landscape thumbnails from imagination), Modular Thumbnail Sketches (build reusable parts and recombine them; the demo subject is robots), Thumbnail Iteration (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/thumbnail-iteration, refining a single silhouette thumbnail with masks instead of redrawing), Chop and Warp (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/remix-your-thumbnails-chop-and-warp, cut thumbnails apart and remix them). Demos use Photoshop but the ideas work on paper by cutting up photocopies.

resources.title: Drawing Basics (Proko): free value and thumbnail projects
resources.free_notes: Drawing Basics is a $159 course with 185 lessons, 58 of them free. Free lessons I could see marked: Project - Notan Master Thumbnails (7:48), How to Organize Values, Project - Value Composition Thumbnails (7:07), Project - Designing Value Groups. The demo and critique videos for these projects are premium only (for example Demo 1 - Value Composition Thumbnails, Level 1, 30:47).
resources.notes: Start with Project - Notan Master Thumbnails: small two- or three-value thumbnails of master paintings, then a self-lit still life photographed and reduced the same way. Then Project - Value Composition Thumbnails (https://proko.com/course-lesson/project-value-composition-thumbnails): at least five thumbnail variations per reference photo in three values. The deadlines shown on the pages (Nov 2024, Jan 2025) belonged to community challenges; the lessons remain.

resources.title: Pictorial Composition (Nathan Fowkes), Schoolism
resources.free_notes: A paid Schoolism course. The page shown did not list a price, lesson count or free preview. Nathan Fowkes' own site says his classes are available as self-study through Schoolism. I could not verify any free YouTube lessons by him.
resources.notes: Named in the brief as a key composition teacher. Page text is a one-line pitch ('great art requires great composition'). Treat as optional; the free sources above cover thumbnailing practice.

resources.title: Muddy Colors
resources.credit: Collective of 20+ fantasy and illustration artists
resources.free_notes: Described on the site as a free online resource with a new article daily, funded by Patreon support.
resources.notes: Look for posts where artists show planning stages that begin with small thumbnail sketches. The home page showed such a post; I did not check the quality of specific articles.

practice.title: Two-value master thumbnails
practice.description: Pick 10 paintings from an open-access collection. For each make a postage-stamp-sized thumbnail using only light and dark shapes, ignoring all detail. Do it in 2 minutes per painting. Compare with the original afterwards.

practice.title: One brief, twelve thumbnails
practice.description: Write a one-line brief (for example 'a lighthouse keeper's kitchen at dusk'). Draw 12 thumbnails about 4 cm wide in 30 minutes, making at least four of them change the viewpoint or crop rather than just move objects around. Mark your top two.

practice.title: Modular kit and recombination
practice.description: Design 8 to 10 simple parts for one subject (roof shapes, windows, towers for a castle). Arrange them in 12 different combinations as thumbnails, then see which three read most clearly at a glance.

practice.title: Cut and remix
practice.description: Draw six thumbnails of a scene, photograph or photocopy them, cut each in two or three pieces, and reassemble the pieces into new compositions. Keep any combination that surprises you and redraw it cleanly.

practice.title: Thumbnail then bigger value sketch
practice.description: Take your best thumbnail from any session and redraw it at four times the size in 3 or 4 values, solving the problems you could not see at small size.

done_when: You can produce 12 distinct thumbnails of one brief in about 30 minutes
Your thumbnails read clearly when shrunk to the size of a stamp
At least a third of your thumbnails differ in camera angle or crop, not only in object placement
You can state why you chose one thumbnail over the rest
You have remixed at least one thumbnail set and kept an idea you would not have drawn directly
common_mistakes: Drawing thumbnails too large and filling them with detail, which defeats the purpose of seeing the layout
Making all thumbnails the same arrangement with small tweaks
Ignoring value and only drawing outlines, so you cannot judge readability
Choosing the first thumbnail instead of comparing at least a dozen

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA (Visual Development emphasis)
school_reference.note: Visual Development is described as high volume with quick turnarounds and needs an art test; students draw props, characters and environments in 2D.

school_reference.institution: FZD School of Design (Singapore)
school_reference.note: Publishes free articles including Sketching 101 and Fundamentals of Design; its programme moves from fundamentals to idea generation to a story-driven portfolio.

title: Reference gathering and building a visual library (with licences)
summary: Good invented drawings come from a stock of real things you have looked at closely. This module covers where to find free, reusable reference (museum open-access collections, free photo licences), how to organise it, and how to study from it without copying a single image.
learning_outcomes: Find usable reference on a topic from at least three free sources in 15 minutes
Tell the difference between 'free to view', 'free to download' and 'free to reuse', and record where each image came from
Build a themed reference board and annotate what you will take from it
Make a small study from reference that simplifies rather than copies
Combine features from several references into one new design

resources.title: The Met Open Access (CC0 collection images and API)
resources.free_notes: Images of public-domain works and basic data on all accessioned works are CC0 (unrestricted use). More than 492,000 open access works were listed. Look for the OA icon on images. A JSON API and CSV datasets on GitHub are provided.
resources.notes: Search the Online Collection for armour, textiles, costume, animals, landscapes, prints and drawings. Filter to Open Access and keep the object number in your notes so you can credit and re-find items.

resources.title: Smithsonian Open Access
resources.free_notes: The page says images can be downloaded, shared and reused without asking and cites more than 5.2 million 2D and 3D items, including National Zoo material. It does not say every item is CC0; the 'Just browsing' link opens a CC0-filtered search, so check each record's usage line.
resources.notes: Good for natural history specimens, skeletons, tools, ships and 3D models you can rotate in the Smithsonian's 3D viewer. Use the CC0 filter if you plan to publish anything derived from it.

resources.title: Unsplash (free photo licence)
resources.free_notes: The licence page says images are free for commercial and non-commercial use with no permission or credit required, but you may not compile Unsplash images into a competing image service.
resources.notes: A fast source of cities, rooms, weather, landscapes and faces. Remember that a licence to use a photo is different from a licence to trace a recognisable person; keep reference for study and invention rather than direct copying.

resources.title: PureRef (reference board app)
resources.free_notes: A stand-alone reference viewer for Windows, Mac and Linux. The pages I opened did not state the price or any free-tier limits; I could not open its support page. Check current pricing before relying on it. A plain folder plus an image viewer also works.
resources.notes: Use it to drag images into one zoomable board, group them and keep the board open beside your drawing. Pricing unverified.

practice.title: Themed board of 40
practice.description: Pick a theme (for example 'deep-sea salvage crew'). Collect 40 images spread across four categories: faces and bodies, clothing and tools, places, textures. Save the source and licence of each in a plain text file.

practice.title: Tiny studies from reference
practice.description: Make five very small studies (about 5 cm) of five different references, each time simplifying a photo down to its main colour or value patches rather than detail. Ctrl+Paint's The Tiny Study video shows the idea.

practice.title: Three references, one new design
practice.description: Take three unrelated references (a beetle, a cathedral window, a coat). Pull one shape or idea from each and combine them into a new object or creature in four thumbnails.

practice.title: Weekly library top-up
practice.description: Once a week spend 15 minutes adding 10 new images to your board from a category you rarely draw (maritime, insects, machinery, ceramics).

done_when: You can find and save a dozen relevant images on any topic from free, reusable sources within 15 minutes
Every image in your board has a recorded source and licence note
You have made at least five simplified studies from reference and not one of them is a copy
You can explain the difference between a free-to-view image and a CC0 image
common_mistakes: Collecting hundreds of images without ever drawing from them
Copying one photo closely instead of drawing from several and inventing
Treating 'free to view online' as permission to reuse or publish
Only collecting references in the subjects you already like

school_reference.institution: FZD School of Design (Singapore)
school_reference.note: Its second term is described as expanding the student's visual library by studying history, culture and nature and generating ideas from real-world references.

title: Prompt lists, drawing challenges and random generators
summary: Prompt lists and generators give you a reason to start and a reason to stop. This module shows how to use Inktober-style lists, unofficial remixes and free random generators to practise idea generation in a flexible way, without turning it into a streak you dread.
learning_outcomes: Run a short prompt challenge (7 to 31 days) on a schedule you can keep
Use a random generator to create a brief and turn it into a drawing
Combine several prompts into one coherent picture
Understand who owns the lists and what the Inktober name can and cannot be used for
Keep a light weekly reflection instead of heavy note-taking

resources.title: The Official Inktober 2026 Prompt List
resources.credit: Inktober was started by Jake Parker; post by Lisa F on SVSLearn
resources.free_notes: The article is public and says following the list is optional. The prompt words appear to be in an image that I could not read, so open the page to see them. The site also sells memberships and mentions a free Inktober community hangout.
resources.notes: The challenge: make one ink drawing a day in October, pencil underdrawing allowed, tag it with #inktober and #inktober2026. The list is a prompt, not a rule. The official site's rules page (https://inktober.com/rules) says official lists have been published since 2016 and links separate trademark guidelines for anyone using the Inktober name to sell products.

resources.title: Unofficial Inktober Prompt List 2026
resources.provider: The Art of Aaron Blaise (Creature Art Teacher)
resources.credit: Posted by Nick Burch on Aaron Blaise's site, 1 Oct 2026
resources.free_notes: The page does not say whether the list can be downloaded or reused, and the footer states the site's content is copyright Aaron Blaise. Treat it as a view-only prompt source. The site also promotes paid courses.
resources.notes: A second prompt list for the same month; the prompt words are in a header image I could not read. Useful as an alternative if the official list does not suit you. Earlier years' lists exist at the same site (ink-prompts-2025, ink-prompts-2024).

resources.title: Chaotic Shiny random generators
resources.free_notes: Many generators are available at no charge; some are sold as paid packs through the affiliated store. No terms-of-use section was found, so use results as private prompts, not as material to republish.
resources.notes: Relevant generators listed on the home page: Fantasy Character, Class Mashup, Monsters, Zoomorph (animal-human mixes), Familiar, Tavern, Bazaar, Arena, Combat Terrain, Map, Planet, Situation, Portal. The site has run since 2010 and the author says it is unlikely to add many more.

resources.title: donjon random generators
resources.free_notes: The home page does not state pricing but has donation links only; it says some content is used under the Open Game License. It sets no terms for generated text, so treat output as private prompts.
resources.notes: Useful ones: Fantasy Random Generator (NPCs), SciFi Random Generator (NPCs, mecha, spaceships), Random Town and Inn generators, Avatar Legends random generator (hybrid animals), Microlite20 Random Monster Generator. Ctrl+Paint's Generating Ideas video links to donjon for constraints.

practice.title: Seven-day mini challenge
practice.description: Choose seven prompts from any list, one per day for a week, with a 20-minute cap each. Change format daily (full figure, close-up, environment, object). Stop when the time is up even if unfinished.

practice.title: Prompt remix
practice.description: Take three prompts from a list and merge them into one picture with a clear focal point. Do it as four thumbnails first and pick one.

practice.title: Roll a character, a place and a problem
practice.description: Use a generator to roll a character, a location and a complication. Draw a single frame that shows all three. Repeat three times with different rolls.

practice.title: Weekly three-line reflection
practice.description: At the end of each week write three lines only: what you drew, what was hard, what you will try next. This light retrieval step replaces long notes.

practice.title: Count, don't streak
practice.description: Set a target count for the month (for example 15 drawings) instead of a daily streak. Missing a day then costs nothing.

done_when: You have finished a prompt challenge of at least seven drawings in a row of days or a month-long count
You can turn a random generator result into a drawing brief in under two minutes
You have used at least two prompts together in a single image
You know the Inktober name is trademarked for selling products and that the prompt list is optional
common_mistakes: Treating the challenge as an all-or-nothing streak and quitting after one missed day
Polishing each prompt for hours so the challenge becomes unsustainable
Posting or selling work under the Inktober name without checking its trademark guidelines
Using only prompts you already find easy

title: Shape language and silhouette
summary: Shape language is the idea that circles, squares and triangles carry different feelings, and that a strong character reads from its outline alone. You design many silhouettes quickly, test whether they read at small size, and learn to use shape families to hint at personality.
learning_outcomes: Design a character or object from a dominant shape family and explain the effect
Produce 20 distinct silhouettes in a short session
Test silhouettes for readability at thumbnail size and by showing them to others
Vary proportion, mass and posture to change the personality of a design
Avoid symmetrical, static silhouettes with arms at the sides

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Thumbnail Iteration (character silhouettes) and The Danger of Painting Silhouettes
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. This lesson page does not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Thumbnail Iteration shows a variation on silhouette thumbnailing: instead of drawing silhouette after silhouette hoping one works, refine one promising thumbnail with masks. It credits the idea to the book The Skillful Huntsman and points to The Danger of Painting Silhouettes (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/the-danger-of-painting-silhouettes, listed under Study Habits; I did not open it). This resource is about the silhouette process, not the meaning of shape families; see the Aaron Blaise livestream for that.

resources.title: The Art of Animation with Aaron Blaise: Character Design and Storytelling (live stream)
resources.free_notes: Published 18 March 2025. The page shows no price or paywall but does not state that it is free, and no duration is shown.
resources.notes: Aaron sketches animal characters from books and film and discusses shape language, animation fundamentals and using live-action reference, plus his Disney film work. Watch for how he simplifies a character to a few shapes first.

resources.title: Character Design with Aaron Blaise (paid course)
resources.provider: The Art of Aaron Blaise (Creature Art Teacher)
resources.free_notes: Shown at $35 (sale, from $75) with lifetime downloads $5 extra; the page says 20+ video lessons and 16-18+ hours (figures conflict). Two preview excerpts are embedded but no lesson is labelled free. The listed topics include making clear silhouettes and using straights and curves; shape language is not named as a topic.
resources.notes: Optional paid extension. Part 1 covers silhouettes, straights and curves, line of action, expressions, eyes, perspective, caricature, costumes and props; Part 2 designs characters for Peter and the Wolf.

resources.title: Storytelling Portraits (Proko)
resources.free_notes: Full course $49 for 18 lessons (about 4.5 hours). Only one lesson is free: The 10 Head Volumes. The rest is premium.
resources.notes: Students design faces for seven animal-based archetypes (lion, bear, ox, snake, fox, owl, pup) in male and female versions, then a full character portrait. A paid way to practise using animal shape cues to express personality.

practice.title: Circle, square, triangle cast
practice.description: Design three characters (for example a baker, a guard, a thief) where the first is built mostly from circles, the second from squares, the third from triangles. Do three silhouettes of each shape family in black, then pick the clearest per family.

practice.title: Twenty silhouettes, one brief
practice.description: Pick a role (lighthouse keeper, space postman). Fill 20 black silhouettes at about 4 cm tall in 30 minutes, varying proportion, hat or hair shape, tool, pose and posture. Cross out any that look alike.

practice.title: Stamp-size readability test
practice.description: Shrink your silhouettes to stamp size (zoom out or hold the page at arm's length) and rank them for readability. Show five to a friend and ask what each character does for a living.

practice.title: One body, five personalities
practice.description: Keep one character's basic job and change only head size, torso shape and stance to make it read as timid, bossy, sleepy, cunning and jolly. Five silhouettes.

practice.title: Animal archetype plus occupation
practice.description: Pick an animal (owl, fox, bear) and an occupation (cook, pilot). Draw six silhouettes that blend the two without becoming a realistic animal.

done_when: You can fill a page with 20 different silhouettes for one brief in about 30 minutes
At stamp size, a stranger can tell your characters apart and roughly guess their role
You can explain what your dominant shape choice is meant to communicate for each design
You have deliberately broken the shape rules at least once and can say why it worked
common_mistakes: Treating shape-to-personality as strict rules rather than tendencies
Putting detail inside the outline and ignoring the outer edge
Making all characters the same height and mass, so the cast does not contrast
Using stiff front-facing poses with arms at the sides, which hides the silhouette

school_reference.institution: Swinburne University of Technology (Melbourne), Bachelor of Animation
school_reference.note: First-year semester 2 includes Introduction to Character and Environment Design; second-year semester 1 adds Advanced Character Design for Animation.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, 2D Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: Page describes students creating original characters and worlds with character design, storyboarding and animatics; the gallery shows character design sheets.

title: Depth, overlap and atmospheric perspective in scenes
summary: A flat picture feels deep when you organise it into foreground, middle ground and background and use overlap, size, value and atmosphere to separate them. This module treats depth as a composition tool: you break scenes into layers, then use lighter, cooler, lower-contrast distant shapes to push space back.
learning_outcomes: Divide any scene into foreground, middle ground and background shapes
Use overlap, size change and value steps to create depth
Apply atmospheric perspective (paler, cooler, softer, less detail with distance)
Pick a horizon height and viewpoint on purpose
Explain when to flatten space on purpose

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint Film Studies: Foreground, Middleground, Background (plus Capturing Stills, Gesture, Color)
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. The lesson page does not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Posted May 2012. The lesson takes movie stills and reduces each to three simple graphic shapes for foreground, middle ground and background. Watch Capturing Stills first (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/film-studies-capturing-stills) to learn how to grab frames, then do this lesson, then Film Studies: Color. Also see Horizon Line and Viewpoint (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/horizon-line-and-viewpoint, Aug 2012, with a worksheet) for choosing a high or low viewpoint.

resources.title: Aerial perspective (Wikipedia)
resources.free_notes: Free to read. Wikipedia text is normally CC BY-SA but I did not open the licence page.
resources.notes: Explains that distant objects become paler, lower in contrast, less detailed and less saturated, shifting toward the sky colour, and gives the history (ancient Roman frescoes, Leonardo, Chinese landscape painters). Use it as a checklist for the cues to paint.

resources.title: The Perspective Course (Proko): free lessons
resources.free_notes: 146 lessons (about 38.5 hours); 32 are free (28 in Part 1, 4 in Part 2). The full course is about $261 at the discount I saw. The page lists a lesson called Depth Tricks and Old Masters; I could not tell whether that one is free. It does not list atmospheric perspective or overlap as sections.
resources.notes: Use only as a free-lesson supplement; check the lesson list for the free badges and look at Depth Tricks and Old Masters.

practice.title: Three-shape scene reduction
practice.description: Capture six movie stills or photos. For each draw a small frame and fill three flat tones for foreground, middle ground and background. Compare how the shapes overlap.

practice.title: Overlap ladder
practice.description: Draw the same five blocks four times: side by side; overlapping; overlapping with size change; overlapping with size change and value shift. Note which panel feels deepest.

practice.title: Atmosphere ramp landscape
practice.description: Draw a landscape thumbnail with five distance bands: darkest, most detailed and warmest at the front; paler, cooler and simpler toward the horizon. Do three versions with different sky colours or times of day.

practice.title: Horizon height test
practice.description: Draw one scene (a path with a house and a tree) with the horizon low, at the middle and high. Notice how each changes what feels grand or intimate. See the Horizon Line and Viewpoint worksheet.

practice.title: Flatten on purpose
practice.description: Redraw one of your deep scenes as a flat poster-style version with no overlap cues, then compare with the deep version and note when each suits a story.

done_when: You can break any scene into foreground, middle ground and background shapes in a few minutes
Your landscape thumbnails show clear distance bands without needing perspective lines
You can list four atmospheric cues and apply them when asked
You choose horizon height deliberately, not by default
common_mistakes: Giving distant objects the same contrast and detail as foreground ones
Placing the horizon in the middle of the frame by habit
Cutting the scene into too many layers so none reads
Applying haze evenly instead of increasing it with distance

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Entertainment Design BS (Concept Track)
school_reference.note: The page lists light and colour, visual structure and world building among Concept Track topics.

title: Environment and scene building: landscapes, interiors, cityscapes and set design
summary: This module is about designing places rather than copying them: landscapes with clear value layers, interiors that imply who lives there, city streets with scale and rhythm, and stage-like sets that serve a story. You work from small thumbnails and simple perspective, using photos for materials and colour rather than shape.
learning_outcomes: Design a landscape from imagination with a planned composition and value layers
Plan a believable interior or street using perspective at the right scale
Use props, scale cues and wear to imply who lives or works in a place
Sketch a simple set (plan view plus key view) for a scene
Use reference for materials and light without copying shapes

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Imaginary Landscape Thumbnails, Horizon Line and Viewpoint, The Tiny Study, Perspective Sketching
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free. Perspective Sketching is labelled a Preview on the library page, so the full version may be premium. Individual lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Order: Horizon Line and Viewpoint (Aug 2012, with worksheet), The Tiny Study (Aug 2012, reduce a photo to colour only), Imaginary Landscape Thumbnails (Aug 2012; make small landscape thumbs from imagination and use a photo only for colour and material). Then Perspective Drawing isn't Scary (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/perspective-drawing-isnt-scary) and Perspective Sketching (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/perspective-sketching, preview) from the Drawing 2 section; I did not open those two.

resources.title: Gurney Journey: Imaginative Realism and Composition labels
resources.free_notes: Blog is free and a January 2026 post says it runs with no paywalls. Permissions allow non-commercial quoting with credit. His books and video courses are separate paid products and are not linked.
resources.notes: The Imaginative Realism label had about 53 posts when checked. Gurney is the creator of Dinotopia; look for posts showing how he builds believable invented places from maquettes, sketches and reference.

resources.title: Marvel's The Art of Storytelling (Proko): Environments section
resources.credit: Daniel Warren Johnson (environments), with other Marvel artists in other sections
resources.free_notes: 130 lessons, 22 free; the full course is paid ($249 list, $199.20 on a sale I saw). The free lessons I could confirm by name are the intro and the expressions lesson, not environment lessons.
resources.notes: The course FAQ assigns environments to Daniel Warren Johnson. Check the Lessons tab for which environment lessons are free; I could not read the lesson list.

resources.title: Interior Environment Design (Will Terry), School of Visual Storytelling
resources.free_notes: Subscription only: $180 per 6 months or $300 per year, with a 14-day free trial that needs a credit card. 14 lessons including 8 videos (about 30 minutes) and a workbook.
resources.notes: Covers designing interiors from different viewpoints, planning spaces to scale, adding props and overlapping foreground objects, and period and location detail. Short; use only if you want a guided interior exercise.

practice.title: Twelve imaginary landscape thumbnails
practice.description: Draw 12 small landscapes from imagination in three values (foreground, middle, background), varying horizon height and the main shape (mountain, valley, river bend). Use a photo only for colour afterwards.

practice.title: A room that tells you who lives there
practice.description: Design one interior (a cartographer's attic, a retired boxer's kitchen) in simple one- or two-point perspective, placing six props that hint at the occupant. Draw it from two viewpoints.

practice.title: Street with rhythm and scale
practice.description: Block in a city street with a vanishing point, then repeat windows, shopfronts or lamp posts with decreasing size. Add three people at different distances to set scale.

practice.title: Set design: plan plus view
practice.description: Choose a location (a market, a clock tower) and draw a rough top-down plan with entrances, then three key views the characters could be filmed or drawn in.

practice.title: Study five places from free photos
practice.description: Pick five photos of real places. Make a tiny colour-patch study of each (no detail), then draw a different place using only the colours and materials from one study.

done_when: You can produce a believable landscape thumbnail from imagination in about five minutes
A viewer can guess something about a room's occupant from the props you chose
Your street scenes hold consistent perspective and include scale cues
You can sketch a plan and key views for a place you invented
common_mistakes: Starting with detail before the big shapes and values are settled
Copying the shapes of a photo instead of using it for colour and materials
Leaving out scale cues such as doors, people or vehicles
Forgetting that the horizon line must stay consistent across objects

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Entertainment Design BS
school_reference.note: Concept Track topics listed include animal anatomy, costume design, light and color, digital painting, visual structure and world building.

school_reference.institution: Swinburne University of Technology (Melbourne), Bachelor of Animation
school_reference.note: Introduction to Character and Environment Design is a first-year unit.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA (Visual Development emphasis)
school_reference.note: Visual Development students create 2D props, characters and environments for games, film, TV and toys.

title: Character design process: reference, iteration, turnarounds and model sheets
summary: A character design is the result of a process: a short brief, reference gathering, many silhouettes, a handful of refinements, and finally a sheet that other people could draw from. This module walks that route and ends with a consistent turnaround and a one-page model sheet.
learning_outcomes: Write a short brief and gather reference for a character
Iterate from many silhouettes to one refined design with stated reasons
Draw a front, side, back and three-quarter turnaround with consistent proportions
Assemble a model sheet with expressions, poses and key props
Build a character whose look implies a backstory

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Designing with Reference, What is Design?, The Reference Process, How to Draw Anything in 3 Steps
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. The lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Designing with Reference (Aug 2012) has you dress provided mannequin drawings as real-world professions (police, firefighters) with specific details, arguing that this builds a visual library for later fantasy and sci-fi characters; it offers a Basic Male Figures worksheet. Read it alongside What is Design? (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/what-is-design) and The Reference Process (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/the-reference-process), which describes how reference photos can play unexpected roles in a painting. The library's design material has no turnaround or model-sheet lesson; see the gap note.

resources.title: Training Yourself to Draw From Imagination, Part 1
resources.free_notes: The lesson page shows no price, paywall or parent course. Not explicitly labelled free, so treat as free but unconfirmed.
resources.notes: Han invents a fantasy character (a dwarf and a hog), explaining his thinking as he builds it, then does line work and ink shadows. A good look at the exploration phase before a design is fixed.

resources.title: Blender Studio: Spring open movie (concept art, character design, model sheets)
resources.credit: Andy Goralczyk (writer and director of Spring) and the Spring team
resources.free_notes: Some blog articles are tagged Free. A related Blender Studio training page (Anglerfish) required a login and a membership of 11.50 euros per month, and said its content is CC-BY. I could not tell whether the Spring gallery items need a login or what licence they carry.
resources.notes: The film page's featured gallery lists environment concept art, a 'Spring and Autumn, character design' image, model sheets, previz images and a colored storyboard sample, plus a 48-minute staff-file breakdown. Treat it as a real production example of what a finished character package looks like.

resources.title: Character Design with Aaron Blaise (paid course)
resources.provider: The Art of Aaron Blaise (Creature Art Teacher)
resources.free_notes: Shown at $35 (sale, from $75). The page lists no free lessons; two preview excerpts are embedded. No turnaround lesson is named.
resources.notes: Part 2 applies the skills while designing characters for Peter and the Wolf; model sheet images appear in the gallery.

practice.title: Brief plus reference sprint
practice.description: Write a three-line brief (who, what they do, one flaw). Gather 20 reference images across faces, clothing, tools and places. Under each group write two details you will use.

practice.title: Iteration ladder
practice.description: From the brief draw 30 small silhouettes, circle five, refine those into rough drawings with faces, circle one, then draw three variations of the head and outfit. Keep every step on one page so you can see the narrowing.

practice.title: Four-view turnaround
practice.description: For your chosen character draw front, side, back and three-quarter views on guide lines for the head, shoulders, waist, knees and feet so proportions match in each view.

practice.title: One-page model sheet
practice.description: On one page include the turnaround, six expressions, four poses and any key props, with notes on colours and materials.

practice.title: Backstory test
practice.description: Show your character without text to a friend and ask for three guesses about the person's life. Change one visual element and see if the guesses change.

done_when: You can take a one-line brief to a refined design with visible iteration steps
Your turnaround views match in height and proportions when overlaid on guide lines
Your model sheet contains a turnaround, expressions, poses and props
A viewer can guess something accurate about the character's life from the drawing
common_mistakes: Designing from memory only and ending up with generic looks
Skipping the silhouette stage and refining the first idea
Turnaround views with drifting proportions or details that do not match
Over-detailing the costume before the core shape works, or copying an existing franchise character instead of inventing

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, 2D Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: Students create original characters and worlds through character design, storyboarding and animatics; the gallery shows character design sheets, environment design, expressions, poses and props.

school_reference.institution: Swinburne University of Technology (Melbourne), Bachelor of Animation
school_reference.note: First-year Introduction to Character and Environment Design leads to second-year Advanced Character Design for Animation and Acting for Animation.

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Illustration BS
school_reference.note: The Entertainment Arts track is described as covering character design, storyboarding, action development and backgrounds.

title: Costume, props and accessories
summary: Clothing and objects are how a design tells you someone's job, wealth, era and habits. You learn to dress a body rather than paste outfits on it, to design props as families, and to use historic and museum collections as reference for shape, material and construction.
learning_outcomes: Draw clothing that follows the body underneath
Choose a few telling details instead of decorating everything
Design a prop in several versions across cultures or materials
Use museum collections as reference for historic dress and objects
Show wear, repair and use to suggest story

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Costume Sketching and Designing with Reference
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. The lesson pages do not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Costume Sketching (Mar 2012) uses fashion photos from The Sartorialist blog as reference for drawing clothed figures. Designing with Reference (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/designing-with-reference, Aug 2012) has you dress mannequin drawings as real-world professions with specific details and gives a Basic Male Figures worksheet. Do both, in that order.

resources.title: Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access
resources.free_notes: High-resolution images and data are released under CC0 for use without restriction; the page says high-res images are available for more than half the collection. The API needs no key and covers over 61,000 CC0 records.
resources.notes: Search the collection for armour, textiles, jewellery, ceramics and costume. Save images with accession numbers.

resources.title: The Met Open Access
resources.free_notes: Public-domain works are CC0; more than 492,000 open access works were listed at last check.
resources.notes: Search by terms such as armour, dress, jewellery or helmet and filter to Open Access. I did not check any particular department's coverage.

practice.title: Dress the mannequin for six jobs
practice.description: Use a simple mannequin drawing and dress it for six real jobs (nurse, baker, firefighter, fisher, surveyor, bus driver), adding three specific details to each. See Designing with Reference for the exercise idea.

practice.title: Read a portrait's clothing
practice.description: Pick one historical portrait from an open-access collection. List five details in the clothing that suggest wealth, job or era, then redraw the figure simplified with only those details.

practice.title: Prop family
practice.description: Design four versions of one prop (a lantern, a key, a satchel) from different materials or cultures. Add one design reason beside each.

practice.title: Silhouette-first outfit changes
practice.description: Draw ten silhouettes of outfit changes for one character on the same body (cloak, apron, armour, tunic), checking they read at small size.

practice.title: Wear and repair pass
practice.description: Take one costume and add three signs of use (patch, scuff, stain), each with a reason in a few words.

done_when: Your clothing drawings show folds and seams that follow the body
Each costume has a few specific, purposeful details rather than random decoration
You can design a prop in at least four distinct versions
You can explain what each costume element says about the wearer
common_mistakes: Drawing clothes as flat stickers that ignore the body beneath
Adding unrelated details without a reason
Mixing eras without research
Ignoring materials, so cloth, leather and metal look the same

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Entertainment Design BS (Concept Track)
school_reference.note: Costume design is listed among Concept Track topics alongside animal anatomy and world building.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA (Visual Development emphasis)
school_reference.note: Visual Development students create 2D props, characters and environments.

title: Creature and monster design: anatomy-based invention, hybrids, fantasy and sci-fi
summary: Believable creatures are built on real animal structure, habitat and behaviour, then pushed toward the fantastic with deliberate changes. You study real skeletons and locomotion, make hybrids that still work mechanically, and design for a purpose and a place.
learning_outcomes: Design a creature from a skeleton outward with joints that make sense
Create hybrids by swapping specific structures rather than gluing parts together
Design creatures around habitat, diet and movement
Use real-animal reference from open collections
Avoid the creature rut of repeating other artists' designs

resources.title: Profile: creature design legend Terryl Whitlatch
resources.credit: Terryl Whitlatch (interviewed); article on ArtStation Magazine, Sept 2016
resources.free_notes: Free to read. The article also links a free creature design course for school students (Creatures of Amalthea) and a 2015 livestream talk; I could not open those links. Her book and Gnomon workshops are paid.
resources.notes: Read for her method: draw real animals from life and from paused wildlife footage; base even fantastical creatures on real anatomy and behaviour; use subtle human-like touches for believability; learn horses, dogs and cats first. She warns about falling into a creature rut by copying other artists' designs.

resources.title: Smithsonian Open Access
resources.free_notes: Page says images can be downloaded, shared and reused without asking; 5.2 million+ 2D and 3D items including National Zoo material. Use the CC0-filtered search to be sure of licence.
resources.notes: Search skeletons, specimens, insects and fish. The 3D Voyager viewer lets you rotate scanned models.

resources.title: Biodiversity Heritage Library
resources.free_notes: The home page states its aim is free access to biodiversity literature. It does not state licences for individual items, so check each item's rights note. The page mentions intermittent PDF generation problems and an uncertain future.
resources.notes: A deep source of scientific illustration plates of animals, plants and sea life from historical books. Browse by animal group to see how naturalists drew form and pattern.

resources.title: Creature Design with Aaron Blaise (paid course)
resources.provider: The Art of Aaron Blaise (Creature Art Teacher)
resources.free_notes: Page showed $45 with downloads (from $70) or $40 streaming only; 14 lessons, 18+ hours of real-time demos. No free preview lessons were mentioned.
resources.notes: Covers anatomy-based invention for bipedal and four-legged creatures, silhouette design, flying and land creatures, mythical creatures, bones and muscles, skin textures, photo-bashing and how environment shapes a creature. Optional paid extension.

practice.title: Real animal studies
practice.description: Make six quick studies of real animals from photos or paused footage, focusing on the skeleton's proportions and where limbs attach. Try horse, dog, cat, bird, lizard and fish.

practice.title: Anatomy transplant
practice.description: Pick two animals and swap one structural feature between them (for example a heron's legs on a bear's body). Redraw so the joints, weight and balance still work. Four designs.

practice.title: Habitat first
practice.description: Write three environmental pressures (dark, wet, windy). Design three adaptations to those pressures and combine them in one creature in four thumbnails.

practice.title: Generator mashup
practice.description: Use a random creature or animal-mix generator, then draw five thumbnails of the result as if it were a real animal. Pick one and add skeleton lines over it.

practice.title: Skeleton to skin
practice.description: For one creature draw the skeleton first, then muscle masses, then skin and surface. Place a human silhouette and a plant beside it to show scale.

done_when: You can draw a creature skeleton with joints that suit how it moves
Your hybrids are not simply parts stuck together; you can explain how weight and movement work
You can describe how each design feature links to habitat or behaviour
You have made studies from real animals as the base of every creature
common_mistakes: Stitching features together without joint logic
Ignoring weight and locomotion so the creature could not stand or move
Copying other artists' creature designs instead of using real animals
Adding features that have no purpose

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Entertainment Design BS (Concept Track)
school_reference.note: Animal anatomy is listed as a Concept Track topic.

title: Facial expression and acting for characters
summary: A character comes alive through expression and body language. You practise simplified faces that still show a range of emotions, then add posture, gesture and context so the feeling is believable and easy to read.
learning_outcomes: Draw a simplified head showing twelve or more distinct emotions
Use eyebrows, eyelids and mouth shapes together, not just the mouth
Show emotion through posture and gesture without the face
Draw subtle and extreme versions of the same emotion
Draw two characters reacting to each other

resources.title: Drawing Character Expressions (lesson 81 of Marvel's The Art of Storytelling)
resources.free_notes: This lesson is marked free (14:02); the full course is paid and has a premium version of this lesson with extra content. 22 of the course's 130 lessons are free.
resources.notes: Covers drawing expressive comic characters using research, simple maths and facial structure. Watch once, then pause and draw along.

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Expressiveness in Your Drawing
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. This lesson page does not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Posted Nov 2012. Argues that character drawing needs expression and body language, not only accurate anatomy, and recommends studying animator Glen Keane's work. No assignment is stated on the page.

resources.title: Atlas of Emotions
resources.credit: Dr. Paul Ekman and Dr. Eve Ekman; designed by Stamen Design; funded by the Dalai Lama Trust
resources.free_notes: Offered online at no charge and asks for donations. No licence or usage terms were found, so use it for study only.
resources.notes: Maps five emotion families (anger, fear, disgust, sadness, enjoyment) with triggers, related states, actions and moods. Use it as a checklist for the range of emotions to draw and for what they lead characters to do.

resources.title: Emoji Based Expressions (Drawing Exercises for Beginners, lesson 5 of 6)
resources.free_notes: This 39:09 lesson is premium only; the full course costs $25. No free preview was shown.
resources.notes: Teaches drawing emotive faces by using emojis and your own face as reference, starting simple and adding detail. Optional paid extension.

practice.title: Emotion grid
practice.description: Draw one simplified head twelve times in a grid, each showing a different emotion. Use the five emotion families in the Atlas of Emotions as a checklist (anger, fear, disgust, sadness, enjoyment) plus variations.

practice.title: Mirror and simplify
practice.description: Photograph yourself making ten expressions. Redraw each as a simple face using as few lines as possible. Keep private images private.

practice.title: Body-first acting
practice.description: Draw eight full-body silhouettes that show an emotion through posture alone (no face).

practice.title: Intensity ladder
practice.description: Pick five emotions and draw each at three intensities (subtle, clear, extreme).

practice.title: Same face, three situations
practice.description: Keep one expression fixed and place it in three different contexts (a gift, a bill, a spider) to see how context changes its meaning.

done_when: You can draw a simple head showing at least twelve readable emotions
Your expressions use eyebrows and eyelids, not only the mouth
You can convey an emotion from silhouette and posture alone
You can draw two characters reacting to each other in one frame
common_mistakes: Showing emotion only with the mouth
Making both sides of the face the same, which looks stiff
Confusing intensity with a bigger pose rather than a clearer shape
Copying an emoji instead of building the expression from facial structure

school_reference.institution: Swinburne University of Technology (Melbourne), Bachelor of Animation
school_reference.note: Acting for Animation is a second-year unit following Advanced Character Design.

school_reference.institution: CalArts, Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: The programme is described as focusing on character performance and storytelling.

title: Storytelling and visual narrative: single-image storytelling, comics and sequential basics
summary: A picture can tell a story through what it shows, what it hints at and what it leaves out. You start with single-image storytelling, then move to short silent comics, learning shot choice, panel flow and how to make a change or reveal clear.
learning_outcomes: Design a single image that implies before and after
Plan a four-panel silent comic with a clear change or reveal
Choose shot distances and angles for emphasis
Show reading order and pace through panel layout
Explain basic story structure with character, change and stakes

resources.title: Pixar in a Box: The Art of Storytelling
resources.provider: Khan Academy with Pixar Animation Studios
resources.credit: Pixar story artists; introduction by Pete Docter and Valerie LaPointe
resources.free_notes: Khan Academy describes Pixar in a Box as a free curriculum, and a 2017 No Film School article calls this storytelling course free. The course page is JavaScript-rendered, so I could not read its current lesson list or confirm it still exists in this form.
resources.notes: Per the 2017 article the course had six lessons: We Are All Storytellers, Character, Structure, Visual Language, Filmmaking Grammar, Storyboarding. Pay most attention to Visual Language and Storyboarding. Confirm the current list on the page first.

resources.title: Marvel's The Art of Storytelling (Proko): free lessons
resources.credit: Instructors include Jim Zub (story), Mike Hawthorne (cinematography), Aaron Conley (page and panel layout), Alitha Martinez (acting), Daniel Warren Johnson (environments)
resources.free_notes: 130 lessons, 22 free (about 35 h 46 m total). Full course is paid ($249 list; $199.20 on the sale seen on 13 Oct 2026). Non-premium users can only open selected previews. The free lessons I could confirm by name are How to Make Comics (the intro, listed 10:17 on the course page and 10:42 on its lesson page) and Drawing Character Expressions (14:02).
resources.notes: Start with the free intro lesson (https://www.proko.com/course-lesson/how-to-make-comics-marvels-the-art-of-storytelling), which previews nine topics including writing, penciling, character design and cover design and sets assignments at the end of each section. The other 20 free lessons are not named on the pages I could read; check the Lessons tab.

resources.title: The visual magic of comics (TED2005)
resources.free_notes: Free to watch on ted.com (16:48, filmed Feb 2005). The licence is TED's CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 usage policy; the policy says use in structured courses or curricula needs a separate licence, so link to it rather than copying or embedding. McCloud's own site lists paid workshops, and his books (Understanding Comics, Making Comics) are paid and not linked.
resources.notes: A talk on the visual magic of comics, presented in a comic-like style, from the author of Understanding Comics. The page gives no detailed outline; watch it for McCloud's framing of comics as a visual language.

resources.title: Start writing fiction (OpenLearn A174_1)
resources.free_notes: 12 hours, Level 1. Free statement of participation on completion; an account and enrolment are needed. Released under a Creative Commons licence (third-party material excluded).
resources.notes: A writing course, not a drawing one, but useful for story basics: character (round and flat characters, sources of characters), setting (including setting as antagonist) and genre. Skim the character and setting sections; it feeds directly into character and environment design.

practice.title: One image with a before and after
practice.description: Design a single image that implies what happened just before and what will happen next (a tipped chair, muddy footprints, an open window). Do three versions and ask a friend what they think happened.

practice.title: Four-panel silent comic
practice.description: Plan a four-panel comic with no words and a reveal in the last panel. Do eight tiny thumbnail plans first, then pick one to draw cleanly.

practice.title: Panel layout study
practice.description: Choose one page from a public-domain comic. Redraw its layout as grey boxes with arrows showing reading order and note where the biggest panel is and why.

practice.title: Six shot sizes of one moment
practice.description: Draw one moment (a character opening a letter) in six shot choices: extreme wide, wide, medium, close-up, high angle, low angle. Note which tells the story best.

practice.title: Story spine beats
practice.description: Write six beats of a very short story in one sentence each, then draw one thumbnail per beat. Check that each frame shows something changing.

done_when: You can design a single image that makes a viewer ask what happened before and after
Your silent four-panel comic can be understood by a stranger without words
You choose shot size and angle for a reason in each panel
You can mark the reading order on any comic page
common_mistakes: Relying on captions to explain what the drawing does not show
Using the same shot size in every panel
Confusing reading order through crowded layouts
Telling a sequence with no change, reveal or stake

school_reference.institution: CalArts, Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: Year 1 includes storytelling and students make a short film each year, with a visiting artist series throughout.

school_reference.institution: Swinburne University of Technology (Melbourne), Bachelor of Animation
school_reference.note: Second-year Writing and Directing for Animation leads to a third-year major project pitched and produced by teams.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, Illustration BFA
school_reference.note: Described as starting with the basics of visual storytelling; student publications include a graphic novel (Meanwhile) and a visual development book (Design Unscripted).

title: Cartooning, stylisation, exaggeration and caricature
summary: Stylisation means choosing what to keep, simplify and push. You practise exaggerating a feature while keeping the whole character believable, designing at different levels of simplification, and learning classic cartoon construction.
learning_outcomes: Push one feature at several strengths and judge where likeness breaks
Draw the same character at three levels of simplification
Construct a cartoon head with volumes and guidelines
Know the difference between caricature of a person and exaggeration of a design
Pick a stylisation level to suit a story or audience

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Exaggeration and Expressiveness in Your Drawing
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. I could not load the Exaggeration page itself (two fetch errors) but it is listed in the library's Drawing 2 section.
resources.notes: Watch Exaggeration, then Expressiveness in Your Drawing (https://www.ctrlpaint.com/videos/expressiveness-in-drawing, Nov 2012; body language and facial expression, recommends studying Glen Keane). I could not read the Exaggeration page, so its content is unconfirmed.

resources.title: Animation Drawing Course (Preston Blair with John Kricfalusi), Animation Resources
resources.credit: Preston Blair (book), John Kricfalusi (commentary), Animation Resources (non-profit)
resources.free_notes: The lesson pages are public, but the course needs Preston Blair's Animation (Book 1), sold separately, plus printed pages from a first-edition Blair book. The book remains in copyright and the site's terms prohibit copying or distributing its material, so only link to it. The site also sells memberships.
resources.notes: Lesson One (Construction, The Head) asks you to repeat a bear head hundreds of times, build an egg model, draw Blair's characters from volumes, compare with the original in red pencil and redraw. Kricfalusi's commentary is on his blog. Only Lesson One was visible on the page I opened.

resources.title: Character Design with Aaron Blaise (paid course)
resources.provider: The Art of Aaron Blaise (Creature Art Teacher)
resources.free_notes: Shown at $35 (sale, from $75). No lesson is labelled free; two preview excerpts are embedded.
resources.notes: Part 1 topics listed on the page include caricature, simple expressions, eyes, and costumes and props.

resources.title: Trove (National Library of Australia)
resources.free_notes: NOT VERIFIED: a bot-check page blocked my fetch, so I could not read what is viewable or any rights statements. Check each item's rights before reusing.
resources.notes: A candidate local source for historical Australian cartoons and caricatures for study. Use only after you confirm what it offers.

practice.title: Exaggeration ladder
practice.description: Draw one face at four strengths of pushing a single feature (0, 25, 50, 100 percent). Choose the strength where it is still recognisably the same character.

practice.title: Caricature from public-domain portraits
practice.description: Pick five painted portraits from an open-access museum collection. For each, find the one or two features that define the face and draw a quick caricature in 10 minutes. Avoid living private individuals.

practice.title: Three levels of simplification
practice.description: Draw one character in three versions: realistic, semi-stylised and minimal. Note what you removed at each step.

practice.title: Construct a cartoon head repeatedly
practice.description: Following the Animation Resources lesson idea, draw a simple cartoon head from volumes and guidelines many times, comparing each with the original page. Needs the source book.

practice.title: Five big shapes from a photo
practice.description: Reduce a photo of a person or animal to five big shapes, then stylise them with exaggeration.

done_when: You can push a feature to several strengths and pick the one that works
You can draw the same character in three levels of simplification
You can explain what you kept and removed in a simplified version
You can draw a cartoon head from volumes without outlines first
common_mistakes: Exaggerating every feature equally, which loses the likeness
Copying one artist's surface style without understanding the construction
Making a mocking caricature of a living private person
Simplifying so much that the character loses personality

school_reference.institution: ArtCenter College of Design, Illustration BS
school_reference.note: Entertainment Arts track covers character design, storyboarding and backgrounds; graduates produce character designs and storyboards for film, TV, commercials and games.

school_reference.institution: Ringling College of Art and Design, 2D Character Animation BFA
school_reference.note: Described as pairing traditional draftsmanship with contemporary production tools.

title: Surreal and imaginative ideation: mashups, chance methods and drawing random crazy things on purpose
summary: This module borrows methods from Surrealism and from random generators to get past your usual ideas. You use chance (exquisite corpse, rubbings, blots), mashups and random prompts to produce strange images, then edit them so the weirdness has an inner logic.
learning_outcomes: Use at least three chance-based techniques to start drawings
Interpret accidental marks as creatures, places or objects
Build mashups from random prompts that still read as coherent
Edit surreal ideas so they have a clear internal logic
Draw many strange things quickly without self-censoring

resources.title: Tate Art Terms: Cadavre exquis (exquisite corpse), plus Automatism and Frottage
resources.free_notes: Free to read on tate.org.uk. Tate site terms apply to reuse of text and images.
resources.notes: Exquisite corpse is a collaborative drawing method where each player draws a section of a figure hidden from the next; the entry says Tanguy, Prevert, Breton and Duchamp invented it in Paris in 1925. Then read Automatism (https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/a/automatism, fast unguided drawing that bypasses conscious control) and Frottage (https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/f/frottage, rubbing a textured surface, developed by Max Ernst from 1925). National Galleries of Scotland has a similar frottage entry (https://www.nationalgalleries.org/art-and-artists/glossary-terms/frottage).

resources.title: Glossary of Surrealist Techniques
resources.free_notes: Free to read on the museum's teachers' resource pages.
resources.notes: Short entries for ten techniques: exquisite corpse, collage, decalcomania, automatic writing, frottage, fumage (candle smoke), grattage (scraping), surrealist object, paranoiac-critical method, rayograph. Pick three to try.

resources.title: Drawing Surrealism (exhibition wall texts, LACMA)
resources.provider: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
resources.free_notes: Free PDF on the museum's site. It is exhibition text, not a how-to.
resources.notes: Describes automatic drawing, exquisite corpse, frottage, decalcomania, fumage, collage and photomontage, photograms, aerographs, and drawings made in response to texts. Read for ideas to try.

resources.title: Ctrl+Paint: Generating Ideas
resources.free_notes: The provider's library page calls its videos short and free; the Premium Series is sold separately. This lesson page appears in the free library but does not repeat the word free.
resources.notes: Posted Sept 2012. Kohr suggests inventing narrow fake assignments, and the page links random generators for sci-fi characters, spaceships, fantasy characters, castles, weather, flags, instruments, arenas and magical familiars (donjon and Chaotic Shiny).

practice.title: Exquisite corpse in three folds
practice.description: Fold a sheet in three. Draw a head on the top, fold it over, pass it on or continue yourself without looking, then do torso and legs. Repeat five times and rework your favourite into a coherent character in a second drawing.

practice.title: Frottage hunt
practice.description: Make ten rubbings of textured surfaces around you with a soft pencil. Find forms in each and develop four of them into creatures or landscapes.

practice.title: Ink blot interpretation
practice.description: Make six ink or watery paint blots on paper, let them dry, then draw into each to turn it into a creature, place or object.

practice.title: Three-column mashup
practice.description: Roll or choose three words: an animal, an everyday object and a place. Draw eight thumbnails combining all three. Pick one and redraw it with a reason for each combination.

practice.title: Crazy hour
practice.description: Set a timer for 60 minutes and draw 30 strange things, never repeating a concept. Keep everything, then circle the five most interesting.

done_when: You have tried at least three chance techniques and kept results from each
You can turn a chance mark into a recognisable creature or place
Your mashups can be explained in a sentence about how the parts connect
You can fill a page with 30 strange ideas in an hour without stopping to judge
common_mistakes: Treating randomness as the point and never editing the results
Confusing 'surreal' with 'random'; a convincing odd image has its own logic
Waiting for inspiration instead of using a technique
Discarding rough results before developing any of them

school_reference.institution: FZD School of Design (Singapore)
school_reference.note: Its second term is described as developing design languages by studying history, culture and nature and generating ideas from real-world references.

title: Visual development workflow: from idea to rough to finished piece
summary: This capstone module puts the group together: a brief, reference, many thumbnails, a chosen layout, a value rough, a colour pass and a finished image, with checkpoints between stages. You learn to budget time per stage and to look at a real artist's or studio's process to compare.
